I... yes, I think we've covered this, haven't we? I know I mentioned it before. There was definitely a time, a few weeks at least, where I wasn't feeling all revved up or grand. I felt quite normal, actually, but the whispers in the apartment were still there. And I was still absolutely certain those arts people were tapping my phone. 

It's so easy for people to tap phones nowadays, with everything being digital. It makes you long for the days of switchboard operators. Have you ever seen those old photographs of the women sitting in rows, plugging those cords in and out? They had to be so quick with their hands. My great-aunt Margaret was a typist in a typing pool in the 1950s. She said the clatter of the keys was deafening, just a constant roar of *clack-clack-clack* all day long. She developed terrible arthritis in her fingers later in life. Her knuckles were all swollen and bent out of shape. It made it very difficult for her to play the piano. She used to play the most beautiful Chopin nocturnes. I tried to learn the piano when I was a girl, but I just couldn't get my left hand to do something different from my right hand. It's like patting your head and rubbing your stomach at the same time. I've never been very coordinated. I took a tap dancing class once in my twenties, and I was always one beat behind everyone else. We wore these shiny black patent leather shoes with the metal taps on the bottom. They made such a satisfying click on the hardwood floor. Hardwood floors are so much better than carpet, don't you agree? Carpet just traps all the dust and allergens. I had this awful shag carpet in my first apartment... it was a mustard yellow color. What were people thinking in the seventies? Everything was avocado or mustard...

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, paranoid belief that 'arts people' are tapping their phone.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient reports experiencing auditory hallucinations, specifically hearing 'whispers in the apartment'.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits marked tangentiality, with their speech drifting from phone tapping to switchboards, typing, arthritis, piano, tap dancing, and 1970s carpets without returning to the original topic.

fully_met.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Are you hearing the voices today?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, I am. I was hearing them just this morning before I came here. It's the whole reason I came in, really, because I keep hearing these very clear voices in my apartment. And sometimes it happens when I'm in the empty rooms at the museum, too. It sounds exactly like women whispering from right behind the walls, telling me which photographs belong in the archive. 

Photographs are so fragile, you know. You have to be incredibly careful with the negatives, especially the old silver gelatin prints. If you get even a tiny smudge of oil from your fingertips on them, it can ruin the emulsion forever. That's why archivists always wear those soft white cotton gloves. They make you feel a bit like a magician, or maybe a mime. Marcel Marceau, remember him? He could make you believe he was trapped in a glass box without saying a single word. It's amazing what you can communicate with just your body language. People don't pay enough attention to body language these days. Everyone is always looking down at their phones, scrolling, scrolling, scrolling. My niece got a terrible crick in her neck from staring at her screen all day. She had to go to a chiropractor. I've never trusted chiropractors, to be honest. The idea of someone cracking my spine just gives me the shivers. It sounds like someone snapping a dry twig in half. We had an old oak tree in our front yard when I was growing up, and during a terrible ice storm in '78, one of the massive branches snapped right off. It sounded like a gunshot in the middle of the night. My father had to go out the next morning with a chainsaw to clear it out of the driveway. Chainsaws are so loud and aggressive. I much prefer the sound of a hand saw, just that rhythmic push and pull. It's almost meditative...

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly confirms hearing clear voices of women whispering from behind the walls, which are auditory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from voices to photographs, mimes, cell phones, chiropractors, and chainsaws.
